extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and critics of poetry (readers learning practical criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, analysing, and judging poetry with emphasis on distinguishing sense and feeling, analysing metaphor, paraphrase, form, and rhythm, and on pedagogical methods for developing these skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words whose feeling dominates context from malleable words
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the distinction between words whose feeling tends to dominate their context and words of a more malleable nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by asking whether the pull exerted by the context is sufficient to overcome the normal separate feeling of the questionable word; examples include 'miraculous' vs 'sprawling' and words cited from Donne and the sample poems. If a word resists the context or 'wrenches the rest of the poem into crudity or confusion' that signals a problem. This distinction explains many mistakes in apprehending feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess contextual influence on a word both directly (feeling) and indirectly (sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of the rest of the poem upon a single word or phrase is exerted in two ways — directly between feelings and indirectly through sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how feelings already occupying the mind tinge a new word and how the transactions between parts of sense in the whole passage control feeling; use both emotional and logical resources to trace these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge poet's power or discretion by reconciliation of divergent feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to triumph over the resistances of words may sometimes be considered the measure of a poet's power, but more often it is the measure of his discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a poet successfully reconciles diverse feelings in context (Shakespeare as example), that indicates mastery; when he does not, the reader should note lack of discretion rather than mere failure of talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that immediate feeling often precedes discursive analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A definite and relevant feeling can be aroused at once, and often the feeling precedes any clear grasping of the sense; apprehension may be instantaneous, and the phrase commonly is accepted or rejected long before the discursive intelligence has worked out the cross-implications of senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss instantaneous responses, but recognise their limits: they can lead to misunderstanding; therefore follow up with analysis to check whether instant apprehension corresponds to the poem's sense/feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paraphrase cautiously — paraphrase can misrepresent a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a paraphrase or gloss for any poem worth reading is a delicate exercise; the risk of supposing that the feelings the logical expansion of a poetic phrase excites must be those which the phrase was created to convey is very great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting a 'bad piece of prose' for the poem. A single paraphrase will rarely indicate more than one partial aspect of a poem; different paraphrases may be needed to elucidate sense vs to suggest feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase to exhibit sense: methods and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase intended to exhibit the sense of a poem requires an intelligent use of the dictionary, logical acumen, command of syntax, and pertinacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utter the word/phrase, note the thoughts it arouses in context, substitute other words from the dictionary to arouse the same thoughts, note samenesses/differences, and construct a definition using well-recognised techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase to portray feeling: different skills required
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase intended to portray a poem's feeling demands qualities of sensitiveness and imagination, the power to use remote experience and to create metaphors — gifts often associated with poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of paraphrase is an imaginative task and may be developable by training, but carries its own dangers; teachers must guard against producing misleading or crude paraphrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the dictionary and vocabulary to disentangle sense
rubrics_metrics.description: To enquire into sense, substitute other words, put definite questions, and choose among methods to construct a precise definition; exploit the syntactical suppleness of language and its overlapping vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot the position of the thought you wish to define relative to related thoughts; this is a recognised and elaborate technique for resolving equivocations of sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits of language for analysing feeling; use available apparatus carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: We have limited linguistic resources for describing feeling (names of emotions, derivative adjectives/adverbs, and projectile/projected aesthetic adjectives) and use them unsystematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to the 'accordances and incompatibilities' among emotional adjectives (e.g., pretty vs sublime); note that qualifying words are often metaphorical and their analogies may be remote—scrutinise what is actually being said about a feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sense-metaphor from emotive-metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense metaphor shifts a word by analogy of objects (justified by similarity); an emotive metaphor shifts a word by similarity between the feelings the new and normal situations arouse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse examples (e.g., 'swine' used for features vs for feelings toward a person); recognise that both shifts can combine. This distinction is essential for describing feelings accurately and for critic's explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor analysis is a critic's technical task
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a writer may use a metaphor and a reader take both its sense and feeling correctly without explaining how it works, explicit explanations of how metaphors work are a special branch of the critic's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should attempt to analyse the ground of the transfer (the resemblance or analogy) even when writers/readers cannot; be aware that creating metaphors is different from analysing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate metrical regularity with poetic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that regularity is the merit of verse is misleading; many finest verses are frequently irregular and do not conform to rigid prescriptive patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of classical-training by-products that teach verse as fitting a framework of rules. An arrangement of departures from and returns to pattern is often the secret of rhythm, but this view is still superficial because it treats rhythm as a property of sound alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate rhythm as interaction of sound with sense and feeling (mental rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic rhythm is not simply a character of the sound of the words apart from their effects in the mind; the rhythm admired is a rhythm of the mental activity through which we apprehend not only the sound but the sense and feeling of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect a physical recording of sounds to distinguish 'good' from 'bad' poetry; consider how meanings and feelings shape recitation. The 'peculiar satisfaction' of certain sounds is a projection of the thought and emotion they evoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both form and content when responding to poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Responding to the form of poetry is as difficult as grasping its content; half the feeling poetry carries comes through its form and through interaction of form and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need reasonable ideas about movement of words in verse; listening to a good speaker can help, but conceptual understanding of form and rhythm is essential to avoid being at the mercy of authoritative readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analysis of poetic compression and instantaneity with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language is compressed and tightly woven, which may obstruct discursive intelligence but assist immediate apprehension; readers often apprehend more than they can later recall or articulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise three possibilities for instant apprehension (fast intuition, temporary 'dissociation' while reading, and compression assisting instant grasp); nevertheless, use analytic methods to correct false understandings and cultivate explanatory habits.
